About

A job board that attracts applicants: candidates browse vacancies and apply.

Challenge

Increase the conversion to applications without lowering the quality of filled-in profiles.
Do it with minimal resources.

Result

+14% visitor-to-application conversion

Year over year, compared with the same period

  • Search
  • Returning visitors
  • Involvement blocks
  • Application form

Search

Findings

24% of users left the site after seeing search results.
Some searches returned no results. The location field looked mandatory, so users didn’t see jobs in neighbouring cantons, even though some were ready to commute there.
The site isn’t a job aggregator and has fewer than 10k vacancies, so filtering too early cuts the results down.

Solution

We reworked the search field: location became an optional filter.
Users can also widen the search with a radius around the chosen cities (+30 km), so jobs in neighbouring cantons show up too.

Before

After

Result

−26% searches with no results

Features for returning visitors

Findings

Returning users made up 38% of all traffic, but the site had nothing for this audience.

Solution

We added two features for returning visitors:

/ previous search/ viewed vacancies

Involvement blocks

Findings

The home page was the most common entry point, but 21% of users left right there.

Solution

Show users more useful information:

  • The latest vacancies, filtered by field and location
  • Vacancy statistics by city and industry

Application form

Findings

55% of visitors left this page without filling in the form.
To find a solution, we analysed how recruiters process applications, and found one more issue: recruiters often had to ask applicants for references and certificates separately, because they weren’t attached to the application.

Solution

Hide less important fields from the first step.
Split the uploads into document types in the attachment form.

Rebuilding product discovery and delivery

DEVELUX · EDTECH
Role
Head of Product & Design
Team
17 people in four disciplines
Period of time
Mar 2023 – Mar 2026

In short

Only 9% of product initiatives hit their success metric, and a hypothesis took 3.5 weeks to reach release. Over three years I co-owned product discovery and delivery across 3+ products and built a 17-person product design and research team that works in every stage of the process. The success rate grew to 14%, and hypotheses now reach release in 2 weeks.

Before

The product process I inherited: design worked as a service

Discovery & Initiation

Research stayed shallow. PMs ran it on their own, while their attention went to the solution. Ideas reached the team already decided.

Discovery & Initiation

  • Product Manager

Delivery

Designers handed off mockups and moved on. Weeks later they reviewed the build and sent fixes, and developers went back for another round, again and again.

Delivery

  • UX/UI Designer
  • Dev team
  • Product Analyst

Results

Fewer than one in ten initiatives hit their success metric, and shipping one took 3.5 weeks. Most of the effort went into things that didn’t move the business.

9%

Initiative success rate

3.5weeks

Hypothesis to release, median

After

The product process we built: product, design and research own it together

Discovery

PMs no longer started from scratch. We gave them a shared insight hub built from surveys and interviews — and researchers who turned it into opportunity trees and hypotheses with them.

Discovery

  • UX Researcher
  • Product Manager

Ideation & Filtering

PMs got partners: the PM owned the problem, the designer the solution, the researcher the insights. Together they filtered ideas with research and product data before development.

Ideation & Filtering

  • Product Designer
  • Product Manager
  • UX Researcher
  • Product Analyst

Delivery

Designers stayed with developers through to release. A shared hypothesis-to-release goal and direct syncs cut rework and made builds faster and closer to the design.

Delivery

  • Product Designer
  • UX Writer
  • Dev team
  • Product Analyst

Results

Three changes drove it: a shared insight hub, a filtering stage before development, and design working side by side with developers.

+56%

14%

Initiative success rate

−43%

2weeks

The UX ecosystem behind the product teams

  • UX Research

    Lead + 4 researchers

    A shared insight hub, opportunity trees and tested hypotheses

    4 designers

What I owned

  • Strategy & goals

    Co-set product strategy and priorities for 3+ products, and turned company OKRs into quarterly goals each person could act on. Our vision, to know customers before, during and after they use the product, is why we built the insight hub.

  • Quality & standards

    Hard-skill standards for each role, checked at every review. Everyone knew what they’d be asked for.

  • Delivery

    Inputs, outputs and checkpoints for every stage of the product process, agreed with every team involved. The process above runs on it.

  • People & culture

    A competency model for hiring and growth, and habits that made us easy to work with: a handoff counts only once someone picks it up.

Acquisition

The challenge

Show that the app can be grown with paid ads at all: find audiences that bring a healthy CAC and LTV. We launched in the low season and chose not to wait for the peak. The whole ad budget for the test was about $52k, so the goal was to find working audiences, not to scale.

Blended CAC by stage

  1. LaunchSearching for working creatives and audiences on a small budget.
  2. SearchBurning through angles and audiences to find a combination that converts.
  3. Audience foundInsight: nurses. Tagging every customer by the materials they uploaded showed nursing most often, though we never targeted it.
  4. Volume testFull launch on the nursing audience, with a funnel and creatives built for it. Switched to intro offers.

Blended CAC: all ad spend on Meta and Apple Search Ads divided by new subscriptions.

Creatives that worked

Share of purchases by angle

  1. Lots of reading, no time41%
  2. I reread and forget17%
  3. Turn reading into listening12%
  4. Eye strain6%
  5. Exams, NCLEX6%

~1%of creatives brought 75% of purchases

Meta attribution.

A funnel built around the audience

  • A separate funnel and a custom App Store product page for nurses
  • 17 quiz screens before the paywall
  • Easy start: age, work, reading time, goals
  • People rate their own pain points: losing focus, rereading, phone distractions
  • The app is set up before paying: voice, speed, reading mode, highlights, quiz frequency
  • A personal plan right before the price
  • Core audience: 35–44 years old, 40% of quiz takers and the best conversion, 7.4%
  • ADHD and dyslexia answers converted best: up to 11% vs 6.8% on average

About 1 in 4 visitors started the quiz, and 86% of them reached the plans. 6.8% of everyone who answered bought.

Web, paid by card. LTV: predicted revenue per customer over 13 months, before fees. CAC: ad spend per new subscriber while the test was live.

Failed payments

25%of web renewals failed on payment

Failed charges were the biggest single reason for churn: 28% of cancellations. I broke every declined renewal down by its Stripe decline code. 58% were soft declines that could be charged again later, and 42% needed a new card. That set the fix: retries on other days for soft declines and a card-update email for hard ones.

Why web renewals were declined

Soft, can retry 58%

  1. Insufficient funds33%
  2. Try again later17%
  3. Declined without a reason8%

Hard, new card needed 42%

  1. Invalid account21%
  2. Transaction not allowed12%
  3. Lost or stolen card8%

Engagement

What we tracked

  • Depth: minutes listened and quiz answers per week
  • Activation: a new subscriber listened 30+ minutes in total
  • Frequency: coming back to learn in weeks 2 and 3. These people stay because the app helps them, not because they forgot to cancel

What we shipped

  • InputKeep OriginalSmart Cleanup adapted text for TTS and filled in gaps between pages. After uploading, people listened less than we expected. We added a mode that keeps the original text and only removes clutter like headers and page numbers. Users split about evenly between the two.
  • PlayerNew player coreText highlighting fell out of sync with audio. After the rebuild, player stalls dropped from about 57 to under 1 per 100 listening sessions.
  • QuizzesQuizzes as a separate featurePeople finished their material and scrolled straight to the quizzes. We gave quizzes their own tab, so a finished text can be practiced right away. Quiz answers grew from about 800 to 2,600–3,500 a week.

What we planned next

  • Kindle integrationConnect a Kindle library and turn any book into audio, the way ElevenReader does.
  • Content from a promptGenerate study material from a prompt, so people don't have to find a document first.
  • Follow-up materialOffer a new generated text on the same topic once the current one is finished.
  • FlashcardsShipped, but we stopped before measuring the effect.

Outcome

The test answered its question: Readberry can grow on paid ads. CAC came down from $263 to $68, and LTV/CAC grew from 0.4× to 1.3×. The next question was whether scaling it would pay off.

Scale plans: cumulative result

Plan we presentedPeak investment −$1.9M · break-even month 20 · payback month 36
Leaner planSpend capped at $650k a month, paused in high-CAC months. Peak investment −$1.4M · break-even month 15 · payback month 29

Decision

Stop before scaling: the money at risk was too large for how slowly and how fragilely it came back.

  • The scale plan needed up to $1.9M and paid back only in month 36.
  • Even the leaner plan took until month 29, and 15% higher CAC pushed payback to month 39.
  • After store and payment fees, LTV/CAC was about 1.1×: each ad dollar barely came back within 13 months.

Three winning experiments that grew first and repeat orders

Role
Head of Product & Design (hands-on)
Team
Analyst, UX Researcher
Period of time
2025

Three A/B tests over 1.5 years, each on a different step of the funnel. Pick one to start with

  1. Experiment 1 Offer card redesign Choosing a writer was the biggest drop-off before payment. Each order drew 30+ offers that all looked the same, so I redesigned the offer card around what customers look for. +14%chose a writer+6%first orders+3.5%repeat orders Read the case
  2. Experiment 2 Sorting by repeat rate Writers whose customers come back for a second order moved up the offer list. Interviews showed it was about communication and deadlines, not better writing. +6.9%second orders Read the case
  3. Experiment 3 Step-by-step order form A long form with many required fields became one question at a time, with popular options as one-click chips. +12.5%first orders+6.2%repeat orders Read the case

Long-running A/B tests, all results statistically significant

Experiment 1

Offer card redesign

Context

  1. 01A writer profile is rarely one person: usually it’s a small company, so it takes orders in any subject
  2. 02Orders are cheap, so writers take a lot of them, and every profile shows thousands of orders and reviews
  3. 03Choosing a writer is the last step before payment, so it drives the conversion of the whole funnel
  1. Post an order
  2. 30+ offers from writers
  3. Choose a writer
  4. Pay

Problem statement

Too many customers dropped off at the step where they choose a writer

Research & solution

Based on regular customer interviews, 7 user tests and 5 in-depth interviews

  1. Core problem

    All writers looked the same, and nothing showed who fits this particular order

01All writers looked the same

  1. Insight

    Every writer had a huge number of reviews

    Decision

    A rating based on the last 100 orders

  2. Insight

    Every writer had a high total order count, and it looked inflated

    Decision

    The total order count was removed

  3. Insight

    Greeting messages were templates and didn’t help

    Decision

    Collapsed into a message button with a counter

02Nothing showed who fits this order

  1. Insight

    No sign of how deep a writer’s expertise is in a given subject

    Decision

    Highlights for each subject, based on the writer’s past work

  2. Insight

    Orders are placed close to the deadline, and customers need time to edit the text themselves

    Decision

    An on-time metric: how often orders are delivered on time

  3. Insight

    Customers worried the writing would look too professional for them, or not professional enough

    Decision

    Writers can add samples for each subject

Results

  • Chose a writer+14%
  • First orders+6%
  • Repeat orders+3.5%

Why +14% choices didn’t become +14% orders

After choosing a writer, many customers were surprised that they had to pay right away. Paying upfront is part of the business model, so some of the extra choices still dropped off at the payment step.

Experiment 2

Sorting offers by repeat rate

Some writers kept customers much better than others, so we showed them first

We changed how offers are sorted: writers with a higher repeat rate, the share of customers who come back for a second order, moved up the list. First-time customers saw them first and were more likely to come back for the next order.

Why it worked

Interviews showed it wasn’t about writing better. Customers came back to writers who were easy to work with:

  1. 01Polite, clear communication
  2. 02Quick replies to messages
  3. 03Orders delivered on time
  4. 04Revisions done on time
  • Second orders+6.9%

Conversion from first to second order. Long-running A/B test, statistically significant

Experiment 3

A step-by-step order form

The order form was one long page with many required fields, and many customers gave up before finishing it

  1. 01One question at a time, so the form never looks long
  2. 02Popular options as one-click chips under every field
  3. 03Each answer collapses into a line with the chosen option, so customers see their progress and can change any answer
  • First orders+12.5%
  • Repeat orders+6.2%

Long-running A/B test, statistically significant
